tagline.text: Embrace the Sierra Madre from a rope-net lookout atop limestone spires

items.credit: Bien Orellana Bacarra Jr / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A conservation area about
2 hours

by car from Manila, where rope bridges and spiderweb-shaped viewing platforms link sharp limestone peaks. Accessible only through small, reservation-based guided trails, it offers a quiet, pristine slice of nature.
Masungi Georeserve is a roughly 2,700-hectare conservation area in Baras, Rizal province, east of Metro Manila, at the
47km

marker of Marcos Highway (Marilaque Highway). It sits on a limestone karst landscape at the southern tip of the Sierra Madre mountain range, where jagged limestone peaks carved by rain over long ages rise among tropical forest, creating a distinctive scenery. The name is said to come from a Tagalog word meaning "sharp" or "rugged," fittingly describing the jagged rock formations.
This area was once heavily damaged by illegal logging, quarrying, and squatting. Starting in the

, a private developer and the later Masungi Georeserve Foundation turned land originally intended for resort development into a conservation zone, posting rangers to protect the forest and replanting trees. Small, reservation-based ecotourism began around

, and since conservation efforts took hold, the number of recorded plant and animal species here has grown from around 400 to more than 800. These achievements have earned the reserve several international tourism and conservation awards.

The trail's highlight is a set of distinctive structures installed among the rock peaks: the giant spiderweb-shaped rope viewing platform "Sapot," the large rope hammock strung between rocks called "Duyan," the teardrop-shaped rest stop "Patak," and the summit viewing deck atop the highest peak, "Tatay" — passing through each in turn while looking out over the Sierra Madre ridgeline and, in the distance, Laguna Lake.

Masungi operates strictly through advance reservations that limit both visitor numbers and time slots, and a park ranger always accompanies each group. This means you can enjoy nature quietly without being crowded. Strongly recommended for travelers with some light hiking experience, photography lovers, and families interested in conservation.
Masungi's signature route: over about
3–4 hours

with a ranger, you cross rope bridges and viewing platforms set across the karst landscape in sequence. There's a lot of up and down, but with structures, stairs, and ropes installed throughout, basic fitness is enough.

A massive spiderweb-shaped rope structure suspended atop a limestone peak, and Masungi's signature spot. Carefully walking out onto the net and looking down at the forest and mountains below is a thrilling experience.
A large rope hammock strung between two rocks. Lying back to listen to the sounds of the forest is the most relaxed moment on the trail.
The highest peak on the trail — on a clear day, the summit viewing deck offers a 360-degree panorama of the Sierra Madre ridgeline, Laguna Lake, and the plains of Rizal.
Small caves such as "Yungib ni Ruben" hold stalactites and stalagmites. Rangers explain how the limestone landscape formed and the plants and animals living in the forest.

A longer route walking through areas of forest restoration, where programs sometimes let visitors take part in conservation activities such as tree planting, depending on the visit's purpose. Recommended for travelers with plenty of stamina and time.

If the full trail feels daunting, shorter programs are sometimes offered in season, such as an early-morning climb up the stone steps to watch the sunrise from a viewpoint, or a rock-garden walk with tea tasting — check the reservation page.

From Makati/BGC to Masungi is about
, taking about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours 30 minutes
by car. A one-way Grab fare is about
. Since a return Grab is nearly impossible to find near Masungi, it's safer to book a round-trip chartered vehicle with driver (about
) or arrange in advance for your Grab driver to wait and take you back.
From Cubao or eastern Metro Manila, take a jeepney or van to Cogeo Gate 2 in Antipolo, then transfer to a jeepney bound for Tanay/Sampaloc and get off at the
47km
marker of Marcos Highway (the Masungi entrance). The whole trip takes about
2–3 hours
, with fares around

. You can also take a Cogeo-bound jeepney from the LRT Line 2 terminus at Antipolo station. It's hard to make the early morning trail slot this way, and return trips are irregular, so this isn't recommended for first-time visitors.
From Metro Manila, take Marcos Highway east past Antipolo and continue on; the entrance is on the left at the
47km
marker. The winding mountain road carries many motorcyclists, so defensive driving is needed. There's dedicated visitor parking, but you may need to register your vehicle details when booking.

To visit, choose your preferred date and trail on the official website (masungigeoreserve.com), send a "visit request," and after approval, complete payment and sign a waiver. Walk-in entry is not possible, and you should apply at least a few days ahead. Only one group is accepted per time slot, so there's a minimum group size requirement; if your group is smaller, you can choose a shared trail with other visitors.
The
November–April
dry season is best. Especially in
December–February
, the cool mountain morning air makes the up-and-down trail relatively comfortable, and clear skies give sharp, distant views.
March–May
heats the limestone rocks up considerably at midday, so booking the earliest possible time slot is recommended.
During the
June–October

rainy season, the rocks and rope structures get wet and slippery, and leeches and mosquitoes increase. If a typhoon or heavy rain warning is issued, trails may be canceled or rescheduled for safety, so check the change/refund policy when booking. Even in the rainy season, mornings are often rain-free, and with good luck you might catch a mystical scene wrapped in mist.
The reserve generally operates Tuesday through Sunday, closed Mondays. Weekend slots often book out weeks in advance, and the year-end holidays and Holy Week fill up even faster.

Masungi has no lodging for general visitors, so most people come and go from Metro Manila in a day. If you've booked the earliest morning slot, staying the night before in Pasig, Marikina, or Antipolo makes getting there much easier. Antipolo's hills have hotels and resorts with a view of the Manila skyline (about
a night), and Pasig's Ortigas district has business hotels across a range of prices (about

There are no restaurants on the trail, so bring light snacks and plenty of water. After finishing, it's common to refuel with bulalo or grilled meat at one of the scenic roadside restaurants along Marcos Highway. Heading down into Antipolo, you'll find plenty of shops selling suman (sticky rice cakes wrapped in banana leaves), mangoes, and roasted cashews, the area's local specialties — great for souvenirs. Antipolo's hills also have several cafes and restaurants overlooking the city.
Book at least 2–4 weeks ahead for safety. Weekend early-morning slots fill up first.
Wear breathable long pants and athletic wear, with trekking shoes or sneakers that grip well. Sandals and slippers may not be allowed.
Since you'll be gripping ropes and rocks often, thin gloves help protect your hands.
Prepare 1–1.5 liters of water per person. Using your own reusable water bottle is encouraged to cut down on disposable waste.
Age, weight, and health conditions apply to some sections, so check the requirements at the booking stage if traveling with children or elderly family members.
Rangers often take photos for you at Sapot and Duyan. Bringing a phone strap reduces the risk of dropping it.
Phone signal is weak in some sections, so agree on a precise pickup time with your chartered driver in advance.
The final stretch of the trail is the most physically demanding. Don't rush at the start — match the ranger's pace.
The limestone rock is razor-sharp, and falls can cause easy cuts. Always stay on the designated path and structures, and follow the ranger's safety instructions.
As a conservation area, collecting plants, feeding animals, writing on rocks, littering, and smoking are all banned. Keep noise down and don't play music from a bluetooth speaker.
If you have a fear of heights or a heart or joint condition, check the trail's difficulty level beforehand. The rope bridges and net structures do sway.
Watch for slipping and leeches during the rainy season, and apply plenty of insect repellent.
Since

, Masungi has faced an ongoing dispute between the government and the foundation over land-use agreements, along with controversy over a nearby wind-farm project. Operations may change, so check the official channels for the latest announcements before visiting.
Masungi is 100% reservation-only. Showing up at the entrance without a booking means you cannot enter — complete approval and payment on the official website before you set out.
About
40 minutes–1 hour
by car. A pilgrimage city known for Antipolo Cathedral, hilltop cafes with a view of the Manila skyline, and suman souvenirs.

children.text: About
1 hour 30 minutes
by car. A natural spot in eastern Rizal with a clear river running among white limestone rocks, caves, and the Mount Daraitan hiking trail.
About
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
by car. A great place to eat and rest in a clean city after your trek.
About
1 hour
by car. A scenic camping ground in the mountains of Rizal famous for its dawn sea of clouds, a great pairing with a drive along Marcos Highway.
